text: ACT is not based on the psychology of abnormality, and it is not linked to syndromal classification. Thus, the same analysis applied to a client applies with equal force to the therapist, and therapy is viewed as a relationship between equals. The client is never viewed as broken, or damaged, or beyond hope. Instead, the perspective is always one of empowerment: that a rich, meaningful, values-based human life is available to all. Pain is taken to be part of life, not a foreign entity to be gotten rid of, and progress is not defined by an absolute level of achievement but rather by the incremental choice to embrace the present and to step forward toward a life worth living. Psychological health is defined by that process of growth. There may be more courage and vitality in a person struggling with psychosis choosing to go to the store than there is in the highest paid CEO holding forth at a board meeting of a multinational corporation. This concept of the 'person' is neither active nor passive but rather interactive. At the psychological level of analysis, ACT is concerned with individuals interacting in and with a context considered historically and situationally. The psychological level of analysis blends into other levels of analysis. The individual is an aspect of the whole and cannot be understood except by reference to context. Therapy itself is viewed as a special social/verbal context involving clients and therapists, each of whom is considered within the same ACT model.

metadata.technique_name: ACT View of the Person and Therapeutic Relationship
metadata.culture_notes: Egalitarian therapeutic relationship may differ from hierarchical cultural expectations; adapt while maintaining core principle of human dignity

text: The impact of ACT does not seem to be limited by region, education, ethnicity, or class. It has been shown to be useful with poor, largely minority clients in a public clinic, with poor South African blacks, with jobless African American persons suffering from psychosis, or with poor persons in India suffering from epilepsy. Part of that expansive impact might be due to the model itself. ACT is based more on metaphors and experiential exercises than intellectual argument, which greatly reduces the importance of formal education. It de-pathologizes the person and puts the therapist and client in the same context, without needless hierarchy. ACT does not take a position on the content of experience, whether that is an obsessive thought, a hallucination, or a strong emotion. Rather, the usefulness of different ways of relating to these experiences is emphasized. Utility is measured against the clients' own values, and values are viewed as choices the client makes, not judgments. This is an inherently collaborative, nonjudgmental, and equalizing approach. Values may differ from culture to culture, but the idea of therapy serving the client values in the client's social context does not. In addition to these features that make an ACT model flexible in areas of cultural diversity and social justice, as the ACT model is scaled into organizations they themselves become more accepting of diversity, more open to multiple ways of thinking, and more values based.

metadata.culture_notes: ACT's metaphor-based approach transcends education barriers; non-pathologizing stance respects diverse worldviews; values work honors cultural differences

text: ACT is also increasingly being directly applied to issues of social justice with good initial outcomes. Controlled studies have shown that ACT can reduce prejudice toward ethnic minorities, toward people in recovery from substance abuse, and toward people with psychological disorders. It also leads to higher behavioral commitments linked to social justice goals. The model has yielded good results on ameliorating the impact of enacted stigma on oppressed groups. For example, the internalized stigma suffered by the obese, substance abusers in recovery, or gay, lesbian, and bi-sexual clients have been shown to be ameliorated by ACT. When ACT is applied in the workplace, workers are more likely to demand needed changes of their superiors in the work environment, even if these were never directly targeted in the intervention. When ACT is applied to workers, burnout decreases and a sense of personal accomplishment increases. When it is applied in school settings, teachers report that their relations with other staff become more flexible, collegial, and values-based. The major organization supporting the development of an ACT model is the Association for Contextual Behavioral Science. ACBS puts its own values front and center including the development of a community of scholars, researchers, educators, and practitioners who will work in a collegial, open, self-critical, non-discriminatory, and mutually supportive way that is effective in producing valued outcomes and that emphasizes open and low-cost methods of connecting with this work so as to keep the focus on benefit to others.

metadata.technique_name: ACT for Social Justice and Stigma
metadata.culture_notes: Social justice applications culturally sensitive; address local forms of discrimination; empower marginalized groups through defusion from stigmatizing thoughts

text: There is a growing body of evidence for the efficacy of ACT across a sufficiently broad range of problems to suggest its utility as a unified model of behavior change. A meta-analysis of controlled studies reported on 21 randomized trials of ACT. The average between-group effect size (Cohen's d) was .66 at post-treatment and .65 at follow-up (on average 19.2 weeks later). In studies involving comparisons between ACT and active treatments, the effect size was .48 at post- and .62 at follow-up. In comparisons with wait list, treatment as usual, or placebo treatments, the effect sizes were .99 at post- and .71 at follow-up. It is the breadth of impact that is perhaps the most surprising aspect of the ACT literature. ACT is recognized as an evidence-based method for the treatment of depression, chronic pain, coping with psychosis, obsessive compulsive disorder and mixed anxiety disorders. ACT is known to be helpful in many other areas such as marijuana use, smoking cessation, managing diabetes, and weight maintenance among many others. ACT workbooks are also known to be helpful. Mediation has already been shown in a dozen studies covering the areas of depression, stress, burnout, anxiety, psychosis, pain, disease management, weight management, stigma, and smoking. Successful mediators examined so far include acceptance, defusion, psychological flexibility, and values.

metadata.culture_notes: Evidence base primarily from Western studies; growing international research; cross-cultural validation continuing

text: The ACT in a Nutshell Metaphor is a practical way to explain the entire ACT model using a clipboard. Hold a clipboard at arm's length in front of your face - this represents painful thoughts and feelings. Notice how holding it up this way blocks your view of the world and ties up your hands, preventing you from doing valued activities. This is cognitive fusion and experiential avoidance - struggling with the clipboard. Now lower the clipboard to your lap while keeping it with you. Notice you can still see the world clearly and your hands are free to do valued activities. The painful thoughts and feelings are still present (the clipboard is still there), but they're no longer dominating your life or stopping you from living meaningfully. This demonstrates acceptance and defusion - the clipboard can come along for the ride, but it doesn't need to control where you go. Practice this metaphor yourself first, then use it with clients to show how we can change our relationship with difficult internal experiences without having to make them go away.

metadata.technique_name: ACT in a Nutshell Clipboard Metaphor
metadata.culture_notes: Universal physical demonstration; works across cultures as it's experiential rather than language-dependent; adapt clipboard to locally available objects if needed

text: Creative Hopelessness is a technique to help clients recognize that their attempts to control emotions are hindering meaningful living. The goal is not to make clients feel hopeless, but to help them see that their emotional control agenda is creative (clever, understandable) yet ultimately hopeless (ineffective for living well). Ask clients: 'You've been working hard to get rid of these feelings. How long have you been trying?' Then explore: 'And how has that been working for you in terms of the life you want to live?' Normalize their efforts: 'Of course you've been trying to control these feelings - that's what our mind tells us to do.' Use the Tug of War with a Monster metaphor: imagine you're in a tug-of-war with a monster over a pit. The more you pull, the more the monster pulls back. You could win by dropping the rope - the monster is still there, but you're no longer exhausted from the struggle. The key message: control is the problem, not the solution. This intervention works best when clients are heavily invested in emotional control strategies and opens the door to acceptance.

metadata.culture_notes: Approach carefully in cultures that value emotional restraint; reframe as 'wisdom' rather than 'hopelessness' if term feels too negative; tug-of-war may not be familiar in all cultures

text: The Struggle Switch is a powerful metaphor for acceptance. Ask clients to imagine there's a struggle switch with three positions: ON (fighting feelings), OFF (acceptance), and the middle position (tolerating/gritting teeth). When the struggle switch is ON, we amplify our distress - anxiety about anxiety, depression about depression. The feelings become problems to fix, creating more suffering. When the switch is at the halfway point (tolerance), we're white-knuckling through, which drains energy. When the switch is OFF (acceptance), we make room for feelings without struggle. Ask: 'Is your struggle switch on, off, or halfway?' Help clients notice what happens when they turn it off - feelings may intensify briefly, but then often settle. The goal isn't to feel better, but to feel what you feel without struggle. Use Pushing Against the Clipboard exercise: hold a clipboard against your chest and push hard against it for 30 seconds while trying to focus on the room. Notice how exhausting it is and how much it narrows your focus. Now let the clipboard rest in your lap. Notice the relief and increased awareness. This demonstrates the cost of struggling versus accepting.

metadata.technique_name: Struggle Switch and Pushing Against Clipboard
metadata.culture_notes: Switch metaphor works well universally; pushing exercise is physically experiential so crosses language barriers; ensure clients are physically comfortable with exercise

text: The Leaves on a Stream defusion exercise helps clients observe thoughts without getting hooked. Guide the client: 'Close your eyes and imagine you're sitting by a stream. Leaves are gently floating by on the surface. For the next few minutes, take each thought that enters your mind and place it on a leaf. Let it float by. If your thoughts stop, just watch the stream. If thoughts come in the form of pictures, place the picture on a leaf. If your mind says 'This is dumb' or 'I'm not doing this right,' place those thoughts on leaves too. If a leaf gets stuck, let it hang around until it's ready to float by. If you find yourself standing in the stream or floating away on a leaf, just notice that and gently step back on the bank.' Practice this for 3-5 minutes. The goal isn't to make thoughts go away, but to practice observing them without getting entangled. After the exercise, ask: 'What did you notice?' and 'What was it like to let thoughts come and go?' This builds the skill of defusion and watching thoughts rather than being caught up in them.

metadata.technique_name: Leaves on a Stream Defusion Exercise
metadata.culture_notes: Stream metaphor may need adaptation where water features are uncommon; use clouds in sky, birds flying by, or other locally resonant imagery

text: 'I'm Having the Thought That...' is a simple linguistic defusion technique. When a client states a thought as fact (e.g., 'I'm a failure'), ask them to restate it as: 'I'm having the thought that I'm a failure.' Then ask: 'Notice the difference - what happens when you say it that way?' This creates distance between the person and the thought. You can extend this: 'I notice I'm having the thought that I'm a failure.' For feelings: 'I'm having the feeling of anxiety' becomes 'I notice I'm having the feeling of anxiety.' Practice with multiple thoughts, especially the sticky ones clients fuse with most. Another variation is to preface thoughts with 'My mind is telling me that...' (e.g., 'My mind is telling me I'm going to fail'). This externalizes the thought-generating process. These linguistic techniques sound simple but are powerful when practiced consistently. They help clients recognize thoughts as mental events rather than facts, creating psychological space between the person and their thinking. Use these in-session whenever clients state thoughts as absolute truths.

metadata.technique_name: I'm Having the Thought That Linguistic Defusion
metadata.culture_notes: Language-specific; requires careful translation to preserve meaning; some languages may not have equivalent grammatical structures; test and adapt phrasing

text: Singing Thoughts and Silly Voices is a playful defusion technique that reduces the believability of thoughts through humor. Take a difficult thought (like 'Nobody likes me') and sing it to the tune of 'Happy Birthday' or another familiar song. Or say it in a cartoon character voice - Mickey Mouse, Darth Vader, a sexy voice, or a computer voice. The point isn't to mock the thought but to change your relationship with it. When you sing 'Nobody likes me' to Happy Birthday, the thought is still present but it's hard to take it seriously. This technique works by deliteralization - breaking the literal connection between words and their meanings. It's particularly effective with repetitive negative thoughts. Some clients resist this initially ('That's disrespectful to my pain'), so explain: 'We're not making fun of your pain, we're just changing how you relate to the thoughts about it.' Practice in session first, modeling willingness to be playful. This technique demonstrates that thoughts are just sounds, words, stories - not facts we must obey. Use it when clients are overly fused with particular thoughts.

metadata.culture_notes: Humor varies greatly across cultures; assess client comfort with playfulness; may be inappropriate in highly formal therapeutic relationships or cultures; adapt songs to local favorites

text: The Hexaflex Exercise is a comprehensive practice covering all six ACT processes in one session. Section 1: Be Here Now - guide clients to notice their breath, body sensations, and present moment. Section 2: Pure Awareness - introduce the observing self, the part that notices thoughts and feelings. Section 3: Know What Matters - briefly connect with values, asking what truly matters. Section 4: Do What It Takes - encourage committed action aligned with values despite discomfort. Section 5: Be Here Now Again - return to breath and present moment. Section 6: Watch Your Thinking - practice defusion by observing thoughts without attachment. Section 7: Open Up - promote acceptance of feelings without avoidance. Section 8: Wrapping Up - conclude with reflections on the observing self and present moment contact. This exercise typically takes 20-30 minutes and can be broken into shorter segments. It's valuable for therapists learning ACT to practice the entire model. Use sections individually in sessions or combine them. Record yourself practicing this exercise aloud to build fluency and natural delivery.

metadata.culture_notes: Comprehensive exercise requiring significant time commitment; adapt length to cultural norms around therapy session structure; may need multiple sessions in some contexts

text: The Expansion Technique is a core acceptance practice with an easy-to-remember acronym. O - Observe the feeling: Notice where it is in your body, its shape, color, temperature, movement. B - Breathe into it: Breathe into and around the feeling, imagining your breath flowing into and around it. S - Expand: Create space around the feeling. Imagine making room for it, letting it be there. E - Allow: Let the feeling be there without trying to change it, fix it, or get rid of it. R - Objectify: See the feeling as an object separate from you - you are the space in which it exists. V - Values: Connect with what matters and take action toward it while making room for the feeling. E - Engage: Fully engage in what you're doing, allowing the feeling to be present. This technique teaches clients to make psychological space for difficult emotions rather than fighting them. Practice each step slowly and gently. The goal isn't to make feelings go away but to relate to them differently so they no longer limit valued action.

metadata.culture_notes: Body-focused practice; some cultures may be less comfortable with interoceptive awareness; introduce gradually; acronym works in English but may need alternative structure in other languages

text: The Sky and Weather Metaphor illustrates self-as-context beautifully. 'The observing self is like the sky, and your thoughts and feelings are like the weather. The weather changes continuously - sometimes sunny, sometimes stormy, sometimes foggy. But no matter how bad the weather gets, it cannot harm the sky in any way. The sky simply makes room for it, allows it to come and go. The worst storm cannot hurt the sky. And even when the sky is completely covered with clouds and we can't see it, the sky is still there, unchanging, always present.' Ask clients: 'Can you notice the part of you that notices your thoughts and feelings? That's like the sky - it's always been there, watching everything unfold.' This metaphor helps clients connect with a transcendent sense of self that isn't defined by transient thoughts and feelings. It creates a safe psychological space from which to observe difficult content. Use this when clients feel overwhelmed or defined by their problems. Practice this metaphor yourself until it feels natural, then introduce it when clients need perspective on their internal experiences.

metadata.technique_name: Sky and Weather Metaphor for Self-as-Context
metadata.culture_notes: Sky metaphor generally universal; however, meaning of weather varies by climate; adapt to local weather patterns and their significance

text: The Chessboard Metaphor is another powerful metaphor for self-as-context. 'Imagine your mind is like a chessboard that goes on forever in all directions. On this board there's a battle going on between the white pieces (positive thoughts and feelings like confidence, joy, calmness) and the black pieces (negative thoughts and feelings like fear, sadness, anger). Your whole life you've been trying to help the white pieces win, but the battle never ends. Here's the thing: you are not any of the pieces. You are the board itself. The board holds all the pieces - it doesn't favor white or black. No matter how intense the battle gets, the board itself is never harmed. All the pieces - good and bad - can be on the board without threatening it.' Ask: 'What would it be like to be the board instead of caught up in the battle between the pieces?' This helps clients step back from the content of their thoughts and feelings and recognize themselves as the context or space in which these experiences occur. It reduces the need to fight or avoid internal experiences.

metadata.culture_notes: Chess not universally known; substitute with locally familiar board games (checkers, go, local strategy games); maintain concept of board vs pieces

text: The Continuous You Exercise builds awareness of self-as-context through experiential noticing. Guide clients: 'Notice your breath... Notice that you are noticing your breath... Now notice the thoughts going through your mind... Notice that you are noticing your thoughts... Notice the feelings in your body... Notice that you are noticing your feelings... Notice sounds around you... Notice that you are noticing sounds... Everything you're noticing changes - the breath, thoughts, feelings, sounds - but notice that the part of you that notices doesn't change. That's your observing self. It's been there your whole life, unchanged. When you were five years old, noticing the world, that same sense of awareness was there. When you're ninety, it will still be there.' Pause between each instruction. This builds experiential contact with self-as-context. After the exercise, ask: 'What did you notice about that noticing part?' This practice helps clients distinguish between the content of awareness (thoughts, feelings) and awareness itself.

metadata.culture_notes: Abstract concept challenging across cultures; use concrete examples; emphasize experiential over conceptual understanding; some cultures have existing contemplative practices that align well

text: Values Clarification Techniques help clients connect with what truly matters. The Funeral Exercise: 'Imagine your funeral. Who would you want to be there? What would you want them to say about you? What kind of person would you want to have been? How would you want to have treated others?' This exercise cuts through surface-level wants to deeper values. The 80th Birthday Exercise: 'Imagine you're celebrating your 80th birthday surrounded by loved ones. Looking back, what do you hope you will have stood for? What do you hope mattered most to you?' The Magic Wand Exercise: 'If I had a magic wand and could take away all your anxiety/depression/pain, what would you do with your life? Where would you go? What relationships would you pursue?' Values Writing: Have clients write about their deepest values in key life domains - relationships, work, personal growth, health, leisure. The goal is not to generate a list but to help clients contact the feeling of what matters. Values clarification should be experiential and emotional, not just intellectual. Connect values work to committed action.

metadata.culture_notes: Funeral/death imagery may be taboo or uncomfortable in some cultures; adapt to cultural views on mortality; individualistic exercises may need reframing for collectivist values; include family/community where relevant

text: Distinguishing Values from Goals is crucial in ACT. Values are ongoing qualities of action (like being loving, honest, or adventurous) - they're like a compass direction you can always move toward. Goals are specific achievements (like getting married, losing 20 pounds, or finishing a degree) - they're like destinations you reach. Values can be lived in this moment; goals are in the future. You can achieve a goal, but you never 'finish' a value. Use this explanation: 'Being a loving father is a value - there's always more you could do to express that. Having a conversation with your son tonight is a goal - something specific you can complete.' Help clients convert goals into underlying values by asking: 'Why does that goal matter? What quality would you be expressing if you achieved it?' For example, 'lose weight' might reflect values of health, self-care, or vitality. 'Get a promotion' might reflect values of contribution, growth, or providing for family. Values motivate sustainable action because the reinforcement is intrinsic and ongoing. Goals without values underneath them lose motivational power once achieved.

metadata.culture_notes: Goal-orientation varies across cultures; some cultures emphasize being over doing; balance values clarification with cultural context

text: Committed Action involves setting SMART goals linked to values and addressing barriers. SMART goals are: Specific (exactly what will you do?), Meaningful (connected to values), Adaptive (moves you toward the life you want), Realistic (achievable with current resources), and Time-framed (when will you do it?). Ask clients: 'What's one small step you could take this week in the direction of [value]?' Break large goals into tiny steps. Behavioral activation techniques are used extensively - scheduling activities, exposure exercises, skill-building. Always connect actions to values: 'Why does this matter to you?' Address barriers through ACT processes: if fusion is the barrier, practice defusion; if avoidance, practice acceptance; if unclear direction, clarify values. The Willingness Scale: 'On a scale of 0-10, how willing are you to make room for the discomfort this action might bring?' Don't push for high willingness - even 3 or 4 is enough to start. When clients don't follow through, respond with curiosity not judgment: 'What showed up that got in the way? What did you do instead? What could we do differently?'

metadata.culture_notes: Action orientation varies by culture; balance doing with being; SMART acronym may need translation; goal-setting may be more communal in collectivist cultures

text: The Passengers on the Bus Metaphor integrates all ACT processes. 'Imagine you're driving a bus (your life), and you get to choose the direction (values). But on the bus are passengers (your thoughts and feelings) - there's the Anxiety passenger, the Self-Doubt passenger, the Anger passenger. These passengers are loud and obnoxious. They yell at you: 'You can't drive that way! Turn around! You're going to crash!' They make threats and even come up behind you while you're driving. You have three choices: 1) Stop the bus and argue with the passengers (fusion and struggle); 2) Do what they tell you and change direction to shut them up (avoidance); or 3) Let them yell and keep driving in your valued direction (acceptance and defusion). The passengers never get off the bus - they're part of the human experience. But you don't have to let them drive.' Use this in group settings where members can role-play passengers while one person practices driving. This metaphor demonstrates that we can take valued action while thoughts and feelings are present and uncomfortable. It's not about getting rid of passengers but about who's driving the bus.

metadata.technique_name: Passengers on the Bus Integration Metaphor
metadata.culture_notes: Bus/driving metaphor Western-centric; adapt to local transportation (train, boat, rickshaw, etc.); maintain core concept of choosing direction while passengers come along

text: Workability is ACT's central pragmatic concept and most useful intervention tool. Instead of asking 'Is this thought true?' ask 'Is this thought workable? Is it helping you create the life you want?' Instead of 'Are you right to feel this way?' ask 'When you act on this feeling, does it work to give you the life you want?' This shifts from truth/validity to usefulness. Use workability questions throughout therapy: 'How's that working for you?' 'If you keep doing what you're doing, where will you be in five years?' 'On a scale of 0-10, how effective is your life right now?' Workability helps with creative hopelessness: explore long-term costs of control strategies. It helps with defusion: 'When you get caught up in that thought, how does it affect what you do?' It helps with resistance: 'Is arguing with me right now working to help you get what you want from therapy?' The key is to be genuinely curious and non-judgmental, not to prove the client wrong. Workability empowers clients to evaluate their own behavior against their own values rather than against the therapist's standards or social norms.

metadata.culture_notes: Pragmatic approach fits well across cultures; however, definition of 'working' may vary; ensure client defines success not therapist; respect cultural values

text: Mindfulness of the Breath is a foundational present-moment practice. Guide clients: 'Bring your attention to your breath. Notice the air moving in and out of your nostrils or mouth. Notice your chest rising and falling. Notice your belly expanding and contracting. You don't need to change your breathing, just notice it. Your mind will wander - that's completely normal. When you notice it has wandered, gently acknowledge where it went, and then bring your attention back to the breath. Think of your attention like a puppy on a leash - it will wander off repeatedly, and your job is just to gently bring it back, without frustration.' Practice for 3-5 minutes initially, building up to 10-20 minutes. The goal isn't to stop thoughts or relax, but to practice flexibly directing attention and noticing when it wanders. This builds psychological flexibility. Assign as homework: 10 minutes daily of breath awareness. Normalize difficulties: 'Everyone's mind wanders constantly - that's what minds do. The practice is in noticing and returning attention, not in having a quiet mind.' This simple exercise strengthens all ACT processes.

metadata.culture_notes: Breath awareness nearly universal; found in many contemplative traditions; generally well-accepted; be sensitive to trauma survivors for whom breath focus may be triggering

text: Notice Five Things Exercise quickly brings clients into the present moment. Ask clients to notice: '5 things you can see right now... 4 things you can hear... 3 things you can touch or feel in your body... 2 things you can smell... 1 thing you can taste.' Go slowly, pausing between each sense. This grounds clients in sensory experience rather than abstract thinking. It's useful when clients are anxious, ruminating, or dissociated. You can do this anywhere - in the office, at home, on a bus. Variations: Notice 5 things of a certain color; notice 5 things starting with a certain letter; notice 5 details you've never noticed before in a familiar place. The Mindful Eating Exercise is similar: Take a raisin (or any small food). Look at it carefully - notice its color, texture, shape. Smell it. Feel its texture. Place it in your mouth without chewing - notice texture, temperature. Slowly chew, noticing the taste and texture. Swallow mindfully. This demonstrates how much we miss when we're on autopilot. These exercises teach that present moment awareness adds richness to any experience.

metadata.technique_name: Notice Five Things and Mindful Eating
metadata.culture_notes: Sensory exercises universal; mindful eating works across cultures though food choice should be culturally appropriate; raisins not available everywhere

text: The Two Mountains Metaphor establishes the therapeutic relationship in ACT. 'Therapy is like this: Imagine we're both mountain climbers, each climbing our own mountain. I'm climbing mine (therapist's personal struggles) and you're climbing yours (client's struggles). We're not on the same mountain, but we're both climbing. I can't climb your mountain for you, but I can share what I've learned from climbing mine. Sometimes I can shine a light on a path that might help. Sometimes I can point out a cliff you might not see. But fundamentally, we're equals - both human beings dealing with the challenges of being alive.' This metaphor normalizes the therapist as a fellow human, not an enlightened guru. It fosters genuine connection and reduces the power differential. Be transparent: 'You know, when you talk about your anxiety, my mind tells me things too - like 'You should have a perfect answer for this.' But I'm practicing noticing that thought and staying present with you.' Appropriate self-disclosure builds intimacy and models ACT processes. Ask permission before exercises: 'Would you be willing to try something with me?' This respects client autonomy.

metadata.culture_notes: Egalitarian therapeutic relationship may conflict with hierarchical cultural norms; adapt while maintaining respect; mountains may not resonate everywhere - use local geographical features

text: Getting Unstuck with Workability uses the concept to help when clients are stuck. 'I'm noticing we're a bit stuck right now. That's totally normal in therapy. Can I ask you - on a scale of 0 to 10, how effective does your life feel right now?' Then: 'What would need to happen to move that number up even by one point?' This focuses on small improvements rather than perfection. When clients say 'I don't know what I value': 'I notice your mind is saying 'I don't know.' Is buying into that thought working to help you create the life you want? What if you did know - what would you say?' When clients say 'I have no choice': 'I hear how trapped you feel. And you're right that you can't control the situation. But can you choose how you respond? Even if your only choice is between action A and action B, isn't that still a choice?' When clients say 'But it works!' about self-defeating behavior: 'Yes, it works in the short term to reduce discomfort. Does it work in the long term to create the life you want?' These workability questions gently highlight discrepancies between client's actions and values without judgment.

metadata.culture_notes: Direct questioning style may need softening in some cultures; balance challenging with respect; ensure questions come from curiosity not confrontation

text: The Wade Through the Swamp Metaphor connects acceptance to values. 'Imagine something you deeply value is on the other side of a swamp. The swamp is full of difficult feelings - anxiety, fear, sadness, discomfort. You have two choices: 1) Stay on this side of the swamp where it's safe and dry, but you never get to what matters. 2) Wade through the swamp, getting muddy and uncomfortable, but you reach what you value. Acceptance isn't about liking the swamp - it's about being willing to wade through it because what's on the other side matters to you.' Then ask: 'What's on the other side of the swamp for you? What do you value enough to wade through discomfort?' This normalizes that pursuing values requires discomfort. The Demons on the Boat variation: 'You're sailing toward an island you value. But demons (fears/thoughts) are on the boat threatening to push you overboard. You can't throw them overboard - you've tried. You can fight them and exhaust yourself. Or you can let them come along while you keep steering toward the island. Which will get you where you want to go?'

metadata.technique_name: Wade Through Swamp and Demons on Boat Metaphors
metadata.culture_notes: Swamp may not resonate in all climates; adapt to local challenging terrain; boat/sailing imagery depends on familiarity with water travel; maintain core concept of accepting discomfort for valued ends

text: Thank Your Mind is a gentle defusion practice. When clients state difficult thoughts, respond: 'Thank your mind for that thought. Your mind is doing its job - trying to protect you by predicting problems.' Then: 'And if you thank your mind and step back from that thought, what action could you take that matters to you?' For example, Client: 'I can't do this.' Therapist: 'I hear that thought - your mind is saying you can't do this. Thanks, Mind! And if you carried that thought with you lightly, like carrying a card in your pocket, what small step might you take?' This acknowledges the thought without arguing with it. It externalizes the thought-production process and creates distance. Teach clients to thank their mind throughout the day: 'Thanks Mind for that worry about the future. Thanks Mind for that judgment about my body. Thanks Mind for that prediction of disaster.' It sounds silly but works. The key is the shift from fusion ('This thought is true') to defusion ('My mind is producing this thought, which I can notice and thank while choosing my actions').

metadata.culture_notes: Expressing gratitude to mind may seem odd in some cultures; adapt framing to cultural norms around mind-body relationship; may need different metaphor for mind

text: The Getting Hooked Exercise helps clients identify fusion patterns. Use a worksheet with four columns: 1) SITUATION: Describe a situation where you got hooked by thoughts/feelings. 2) HOOKED: What thoughts/feelings showed up? Which ones did you get hooked by? 3) BEHAVIOR: What did you do when hooked? How did it affect your actions? 4) UNHOOKING: Looking back, what could you have done to unhook? What value could you have acted on instead? Example: Situation - 'Invited to party'; Hooked - 'Nobody will like me, I'll be awkward'; Behavior - 'Stayed home, watched TV'; Unhooking - 'Notice the thought, thank my mind, go to party anyway (value: connection).' This builds awareness of the fusion-avoidance-unworkable action cycle. Clients complete this as homework after difficult situations. In session, review: 'What did you notice? When you got hooked, where did it show up in your body? What actions did it pull you toward? What valued action could you take next time this hook shows up?' This develops the skill of noticing hooks in real time.

metadata.culture_notes: Worksheet requires literacy; adapt for oral cultures through discussion; 'hooked' metaphor may need explanation or alternative imagery

text: Rapid Defusion Technique using repetition helps with particularly sticky thoughts. Take a single word from the thought (often the most painful word), like 'failure' from 'I'm a failure.' Have the client say that word out loud, rapidly, for 30 seconds: 'Failure failure failure failure...' The research shows this reduces the believability of the word and the distress it causes - the 'sweet spot' is 30 seconds. What happens is deliteralization - the word loses its literal meaning and becomes just a sound. Afterward ask: 'What did you notice? What happened to the word?' Most clients report it started to sound strange or meaningless. This demonstrates that words and thoughts are just noises, not facts. Use this with core cognitive content clients repeatedly fuse with: worthless, unlovable, stupid, etc. It's brief and can be done in session or as homework. Warning: some clients find this distressing initially, so get permission first and stop if it's genuinely overwhelming. The goal is to help clients see that meaning isn't inherent in words - it's something we add.

metadata.culture_notes: Language-specific effect; may work differently across languages; test first; some words may be taboo to repeat in certain cultures; proceed with sensitivity

text: Writing Values Letters helps clients emotionally connect with values. Ask clients to write: 'A letter from your 80-year-old self to your present self, sharing wisdom about what truly matters' or 'A letter to someone you love, describing what they mean to you and how you want to show up for them' or 'Your own eulogy - what you hope people would say about the life you lived and the person you were.' This isn't about generating lists but about contacting the feeling of meaning. Clients often become emotional during values work - that's good. It means they're connecting with what matters, not just intellectualizing. After writing, ask: 'As you wrote that, what showed up for you? What did you notice in your body?' Then immediately connect to action: 'Based on what you wrote, what's one small step you could take this week?' The writing makes values concrete and memorable. Clients can return to these letters when motivation wanes or when difficult emotions show up. The emotional connection is what fuels committed action when barriers arise.

metadata.culture_notes: Requires literacy and comfort with writing; adapt for oral cultures using recorded voice messages; cultural views on aging and death vary; adjust age references

text: The Problem-Solving Machine Metaphor explains experiential avoidance. 'Your mind is like a problem-solving machine. Its job is to identify problems and solve them. This works great for external problems - if you're cold, you put on a coat; if you're hungry, you eat. But the mind applies the same strategy to internal experiences - if you feel anxious, it tries to get rid of anxiety; if you have sad thoughts, it tries to eliminate them. The problem is, the more you try to control or eliminate thoughts and feelings, the more they show up. It's like quicksand - the more you struggle, the deeper you sink. Or like trying not to think of a white bear - the instruction to not think about it makes you think about it more.' This explains why control strategies backfire. Then: 'What if the solution isn't to fix or eliminate these feelings, but to change how you relate to them? What if you could carry them with you while you do what matters?' This sets up acceptance and defusion as alternatives to the control agenda.

metadata.culture_notes: Machine metaphor Western/technological; may need adaptation to agricultural or nature-based metaphors; quicksand familiar in some contexts but not all

text: Assessing Psychological Flexibility using the Six Core Processes helps case conceptualization. For each process, ask: 1) Dominance of Past/Future: Is the client lost in rumination about past or worry about future? Missing present moment? 2) Fusion: What thoughts is the client fused with? Do they believe thoughts are literally true and act on them automatically? 3) Experiential Avoidance: What thoughts/feelings is the client trying to avoid? What are their avoidance strategies? 4) Conceptualized Self: Is the client attached to rigid self-descriptions (I'm broken, I'm a failure, I'm a victim)? 5) Lack of Values Clarity: Is the client unclear about what matters? Are they pursuing shoulds rather than wants? 6) Unworkable Action: What patterns of behavior are inconsistent with values? These six processes overlap and reinforce each other. Most clients show some degree of inflexibility in multiple areas. Don't try to address everything at once - target whatever is most prominent or most blocking valued action. Use this assessment to guide intervention selection.

metadata.culture_notes: Six processes framework developed in Western context; some concepts translate better than others; assess within cultural context of what constitutes workable living

text: Self-Compassion in Acceptance is crucial when painful emotions arise. Guide clients: 'As you notice this difficult feeling, place your hand on your heart or wherever feels comforting. Imagine speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to a dear friend or young child who is struggling - with kindness and understanding. You might say: 'This is really hard right now. It makes sense that I feel this way. I'm not alone in feeling this - all humans struggle sometimes. May I be kind to myself in this moment.'' This activates the care system in the brain rather than the threat system. It's different from self-esteem (I'm good/bad) or positive thinking (everything will be fine). Self-compassion acknowledges difficulty while offering kindness. It's especially important for clients who are harsh and critical with themselves. Normalize emotions: 'Feelings like this are a normal part of being human. They show up when we care about something or when we're facing challenges.' This frames emotions as information and as evidence of being alive, not as signs of weakness or pathology.

metadata.culture_notes: Self-compassion varies across cultures; some cultures emphasize endurance over self-kindness; adapt language to cultural values; physical touch (hand on heart) may be uncomfortable for some

text: Mindfulness in Daily Activities extends present moment awareness beyond formal practice. Ask clients to choose one routine daily activity and do it mindfully for a week: brushing teeth, washing dishes, taking a shower, walking to the car, drinking morning coffee. 'As you do this activity, bring full attention to the sensory experience. Notice the temperature, textures, sounds, movements. When your mind wanders to planning or ruminating, gently bring it back to the sensory experience. You're not trying to enjoy it more or do it better - just to be fully present.' This builds the skill of interrupting autopilot and choosing where to direct attention. It demonstrates that any moment can be rich if we're present for it. Another practice: Mindful Driving - notice the feeling of hands on the wheel, the sound of the engine, the visual field moving past. Mindful Walking - notice each footstep, the shift of weight, the movement of legs. The goal is to generalize mindfulness from formal meditation to everyday life, which is where psychological flexibility actually matters.

metadata.culture_notes: Daily activities vary by culture and lifestyle; choose activities relevant to client's life; driving not universal; adapt to walking, cooking, tea preparation, prayer, etc.

text: From Chunky to Fluid ACT describes the therapist's learning journey. New ACT therapists often apply processes in isolation - doing a defusion exercise, then separately an acceptance exercise, then values work. This is 'chunky' ACT. With practice, therapists learn to blend processes fluidly, moving naturally between defusion, acceptance, present moment, self-as-context, values, and committed action within a single conversation. For example: 'I notice your mind just said you're going to fail (defusion). Can you make room for that thought and the anxiety it brings (acceptance) while staying present with me here (present moment) and telling me what really matters to you about this situation (values)? What would you do if that thought and feeling could come along for the ride (committed action)?' This integration comes from: 1) Practicing ACT on yourself, 2) Really understanding how the processes interrelate, 3) Being present and flexible with clients rather than following scripts, 4) Repetition and learning from mistakes. Mastering ACT typically takes at least a year of dedicated practice. Attending experiential workshops and practicing with peers accelerates learning.

metadata.culture_notes: Learning trajectory universal; importance of practice and experiential training emphasized across therapeutic modalities; supervision practices vary by culture

text:
This is a good exercise to use when you want to center yourself and get fully present in the moment. You can do it at any time, but you might find it especially helpful when you are caught up in your thoughts or emotions and need to get some clarity and stability before you decide how to respond in a way that's consistent with your values.

1. Take a moment to notice your experience. Notice any struggle you may be experiencing. Take note of where you feel it in your body, also noticing any thoughts, emotions, or urges that go with it. If it helps, you can imagine it has a color or a shape, like an object. You don't have to do anything with it or make it go away. For now, just acknowledge that it's here.

2. Do something with your body. Like stand up and walk around, or have a stretch, or press your feet into the floor and notice how it's firm beneath you. Just check back in with the struggle briefly, just notice it's there and where you feel it, but also notice that you have a body that surrounds it that you can control. Again, do something with your body--- like take a few deep breaths, or have another stretch.

3. Look around and notice the sights around you. See if you can name five things that you can see around you. Notice what you can hear. Name three to four sounds that you can hear around you. Do you notice any tastes or smells? Touch something near you and notice its texture.

4. Check back in with the struggle. Just notice if it is still there, or if it has changed in any way. As best you can, see if you can just let it be. And, again notice that you have a body around it that you can control. Notice the sights and sounds around you.

5. Notice what you are doing. See if you can fully engage in the task at hand. If it's not clear what to do, check in with your values. Notice who you want to be and how you want to respond in this moment and take action. If you are still overwhelmed or still feel stuck, repeat the steps above two to three times, or until you are able to make some room for the struggle and identify a values-based action.

metadata.culture_notes: Adapted from Harris (2019). Useful for veterans experiencing overwhelming emotions or trauma triggers. Emphasizes body awareness and values-based action.

text:
Find some time to sit in a comfortable place, where you won't be disturbed. Sit in a position where you are relaxed but still alert: sitting up in a dignified posture with your back straight, head balanced on your shoulders, arms and shoulders relaxed and resting in a comfortable position.

Consider your intentions in this moment. See if you can give yourself a gift of stillness. This is an opportunity to switch from your normal mode of doing, planning, moving, and reacting to one of simply being. Just notice whatever happens in your awareness, right here and right now.

Just notice the sensations of your breath. Just notice your abdomen on the inbreath and the outbreath. Notice the subtle movement of your chest and shoulders. Notice the air as it flows through your nostrils: cool on the inbreath, warmer on the outbreath.

Pay attention to the entire cycle of the breath. It's all one motion, but it has its phases. Notice the inbreath and the outbreath. Notice the space between them, the pause between breathing in and breathing out.

You'll notice that your attention will stray from your breath from time to time. This is OK. It's your mind's job to wander. When you notice this, as best you can and without giving yourself a hard time, gently bring your attention back to your breath.

See if you can let go of any need to control your breathing. Imagine floating on the surface of the ocean…riding the waves up and down. You don't control how high or low the wave goes, or how long it lasts. Simply ride the waves of your breath.

You may notice there are sounds other than those of your breathing. Sounds near and far. Just notice when your attention moves to the perception of sound. Notice the qualities of the sound: its volume, tone, and intensity. Notice your mind's tendency to label the sounds: there's traffic, someone walking down the hall, the wind in the trees (use your own examples). As best you can, see if you can separate the labels from the experience of the sound, listening with curiosity as if you were hearing these things for the first time. And when you've done that, gently come back to your breath.

metadata.culture_notes: Formal mindfulness practice for veterans. Emphasizes non-judgmental awareness and returning attention to breath without self-criticism.

text:
Notice any judgments that may come up. Opinions about whether you like or dislike this experience, or wondering if you're doing it right. Notice your judging mind and your critical mind if they show up now. And as best you can, realize that there is nothing that needs to be fixed here… you don't have to process anything or work it out. Just notice your experience in this moment. And gently come back to your breath….

You may notice that your attention shifts to bodily sensations. They may be pleasant, like a sense of warmth, relaxation, or comfort. Or they may be more like a sense of tension, or an ache or an itch. When you notice these sensations, there are a couple of options; and neither is better than the other. The first is to notice where the sensation is, how intense or large it is. And, if it's something you need to fix, first form the intention to act, then do whatever it is you need to be more comfortable. For example, you might notice tension at some place in your body, as well as an urge to stretch or change position to alleviate the discomfort. First form intention to move, then do what you need to do to be more comfortable. The second way would be to just observe the sensation with curiosity and see if you can stay with it just for a moment longer. Imagine you can breathe into the sensation. Notice where it is, and what shape it would take if you could trace its outline in your body. Notice if it changes in any way…or if it doesn't change, just notice that as well. Just notice you can stay with it without reacting to it.

So, you have two ways of responding to physical sensations that come up. Whichever option you choose, just notice that you do so as a conscious choice.

Just gently notice whatever comes into your awareness; thoughts, memories, emotions, physical sensations, urges. See if you can welcome each in turn. As you notice each, realize that this is a moment of awareness. And then gently come back to your breath. Just notice the process of coming back, again and again, as many times as you need to, with kindness.

As this meditation draws to a close, bring your awareness back to the weight of your body here in the chair. Open your eyes or look up and notice all the sights and sounds. Congratulate yourself for taking this time for yourself, giving yourself a moment of stillness.

metadata.culture_notes: Teaches choice in responding to physical sensations. Relevant for veterans with chronic pain or trauma-related body sensations.

text:
Taking an "observer perspective" means developing a stable sense of yourself that is not limited by your thoughts, emotions, urges or bodily sensations. This bigger sense of self allows you to notice your thoughts and feelings without judgment. Also, developing this larger sense of self allows you to realize that you don't have to be controlled by your thoughts and feelings, so that you can make better choices that are guided by what really matters to you. When you learn to accept even your most painful thoughts and feelings, you can be kinder to yourself and others. Finally, developing this observer self allows you to realize that, even if you have been through very difficult experiences in your life, there is a part of you that has remained stable and strong throughout these experiences.

Your body is constantly changing. Once you were a little baby, and then you grew into a child, and then that child grew into the person you are now. Your body may become heavy or light, strong or weak. Sometimes your body may be sick or hurt. You may have had illnesses or been injured. Over time, these hurts have either healed or perhaps they are with you even now. Notice these things, but also notice that there is a "you" that has been there all along. Even though your body has changed, the person that is you—the observer—was there all along.

Now, notice your roles. You have many of them. You are constantly playing a role. Perhaps you play a role at work, or as someone who is retired or disabled. You may play the role of a spouse or a parent. You play the role of a son or a daughter. You play the role of a service member or a Veteran. You play the role of someone of a certain race, age, ethnicity, or belief system. Your roles are constantly changing, and you change in and out of them like suits of clothes. Even now you might be playing the role of someone in therapy. If you were to try to not play a role, then you would be in the role of someone who does not play a role. Allow yourself to notice this as a fact that you have experienced: I have many roles, but the roles are not me. You are there all along, observing your many roles.

metadata.section_title: Self-as-Context: Observer Self Handout for Veterans
metadata.culture_notes: Adapted from Hayes et al. (2012). Particularly relevant for veterans transitioning from military roles or struggling with trauma-based identity.

text:
Now, notice your emotions. They are constantly changing. There may be things that you liked at one time that you do not like now. Or there may be things that you did not like at one time, that you now like. Sometimes you may have more than one emotion at the same time. Sometimes these emotions contradict themselves. Even now you are experiencing emotions, but they are not you. You have been there all along, observing these many emotions. The emotions are like waves, but you are like the ocean. Allow yourself to experience this as a fact: you have many emotions, but these emotions are not you.

Now, notice that you have many thoughts. Your thoughts are constantly changing. You have learned new things and have had different experiences from which you have gotten new knowledge and new ideas. Perhaps there are some things that you once believed were true, that you now know to be false. Or the opposite may also be true, that there are things you once thought were false that you now know to be true. Sometimes your thoughts may make little sense to you. They may seem to pop into your head for no apparent reason. Some may have been around for a long time. You have many thoughts, but they are not you. You have been there, observing your thoughts all along.

Notice that you are not your body, emotions, roles, or thoughts. When you notice this, see if you can create a sense of distance between you and the things you may be struggling with…not to make them go away, but to make space for them. Note that you may have been trying to change some of these thoughts, emotions, or sensations. Perhaps you have been trying to get rid of the "bad" thoughts or feelings; but as you do, you may get caught up in them and you do not notice the you that is separate from them. There is a you-yourself, an observer you, that has been there all along. You encompass all these things and are bigger than these things. And you can choose a direction for your life and follow it, independent of what all these other things may tell you.

metadata.section_title: Self-as-Context: Observer Self Handout for Veterans
metadata.culture_notes: Uses metaphors (waves/ocean) to help veterans separate from difficult internal experiences while maintaining sense of wholeness.

text:
Inside/Outside Shifting

This is an exercise to practice deliberately shifting your focus from something in your environment to something internal. For example, you might spend five minutes observing the wind blowing through the trees, the number and pattern of tiles in the floor, or a piece of art or music. Next, you would shift attention to your breath, or perhaps any sensations you might notice in your body, or a sense of pressure or warmth, or the soles of your feet on the floor. Set a timer on your phone, or watch to signal when to shift back and forth between internal and external focus.

Social Inside/Outside Shifting

Similar to above, but practice shifting from noticing your internal experience to the activity of others around you. This might work best at a place where you can "people-watch," like a park or mall, store, or class. Take some time to notice the behavior of others around you, their posture, tone of voice, facial expressions, etc. Then shift your attention to your internal experience of your thoughts, emotions, and urges, and vice-versa. Alternate between inside and outside yourself by using a timer for a signal.

*** If you want to "level-up" this experience, try shifting back and forth from observer to participant. For example, at a work meeting you might intentionally take some time to observe your coworkers, then intentionally engage in the meeting, then shift back to observation.

Now/Then Shifting

Find a photo album, electronic or physical. Pick three pictures from different parts of your life. Ideally, the pictures should be at least a year apart. Answer the following questions for each of the pictures:
• How old were you? What is happening in the picture? What was going on in that time of your life?
• What physical sensations were you experiencing at that time?
• What thoughts might you have been having?
• What emotions were you feeling?
• What thoughts, feelings, and emotions are you experiencing now as you reflect back on this scene?

metadata.culture_notes: Adapted from Strosahl & Robinson (2015). Helps veterans practice flexible attention and reduce stuck patterns. Photo exercise useful for processing trauma timeline.

text:
Start by sitting in a position where you're relaxed but still alert. Go ahead and close your eyes, or if that makes you uncomfortable, just let your gaze rest softly on the floor or the wall. Take just a moment and notice the weight of your body in the chair. Notice the places where it contacts the chair: your back, hips, and arms. See if you can notice the weight of your arms. You may have to let your shoulders relax a bit to do that. Perhaps press your feet gently into the floor if you'd like. Notice the firmness of the floor beneath them. Maybe wiggle your toes around a bit and notice any sensations there. And now, if you'd like, just notice your breath.

Now, if you're willing, bring to mind someone who is dear to you. Imagine that this person is experiencing some sort of struggle, in a dark night of the soul. Perhaps the person is sad, or angry, or afraid. Take a moment and notice the person's facial expression, posture in this moment of pain. Notice how your heart goes out to the person.

Now imagine you can approach this dear person in this moment of suffering. Do whatever you need to get their attention. Say: "I see you. I see you in this moment of pain; and I have known pain, too. May you be free from suffering. May you know peace." Imagine you can physically comfort the person at this time, perhaps through a hand on the shoulder, or an embrace.

Now, let that image fade.

Next, imagine yourself experiencing some sort of struggle, a dark night of the soul. Perhaps you are sad, or angry, or afraid. Take a moment and see yourself in that moment of pain. Notice your facial expression and posture in this moment of pain. Notice how your heart goes out to yourself in that moment.

Now imagine you can approach yourself in this moment of suffering. Do whatever you need to get your attention. Say: "I see you. I see you in this moment of pain, I remember this moment. May you be free from suffering. May you know peace." Imagine you can physically comfort that person who was you, perhaps through a hand on your shoulder, or an embrace. Notice as this person dissolves into the you that is here, now.

And just breathe, gently allowing your breath to breathe itself. And notice your body here in this moment, the weight of it. Notice your feet on the floor and the weight of your arms. Notice any sounds around you. Open your eyes and look up, expanding your attention to take in this moment, and bring this sense of compassion to the rest of your day.

metadata.culture_notes: Particularly powerful for veterans struggling with guilt, shame, or self-blame related to combat experiences or trauma.

text:
Take a few moments to get centered, taking a few mindful breaths.

Now, imagine that you have a photo album before you. It could be an actual book, or an electronic album in a phone or computer. The key is that this album has pictures from throughout your life until now. Just take a moment, and in your mind's eye look through the album. Now, see if you can go to the part of the album that covers last summer. Just scan through the pictures from last summer until you find yourself lingering at a certain picture. Pause and see yourself there. Really put yourself into that scene, as the person behind your eyes in that moment. Notice what you were doing. Who was there with you? Picture all the sights and sounds. What are you thinking and feeling in that moment? Really take in the scene.

Now, when you are ready, leave that scene (knowing you can come back later if you want) and start looking though the part of the album that is your childhood. See if you can find a moment where you experienced some early hurt…a time when you were alone and sad, or afraid. Maybe six or seven years old, but whatever age seems right to you. Really see yourself in that moment. Look down and notice how small your hands are. Notice all the sights and sounds around you. Notice what you are feeling and thinking as the child who was there in that moment.

Now, imagine that the adult you, the present day you, enters that scene. Just picture what it's like to open the door now and walk into that moment. Look on that child who was you in that moment of pain. Notice the child's facial expressions and posture. Take a moment and notice what you feel now, looking upon this child. See if it's the case that your heart naturally inclines to the child that was you. What does the child need in this moment? Imagine that you can give that child whatever it needs in this time of suffering. If it's words, imagine yourself saying what that child needs to hear. Say it out loud in this very moment.

Now, imagine you come up to this child you, and embrace it. Notice what it's like to have the child in your arms. And now, as you hold the child, imagine that it dissolves and absorbs into the adult you. Take a moment now to embrace yourself, transmitting kindness and compassion.

And again, notice your breath. Notice the sounds in the room and open your eyes. Take a few moments to reflect on your experience.

metadata.culture_notes: Adapted from Walser & Westrup (2007). Powerful for veterans with childhood trauma or those who entered military service at young age. May evoke strong emotions.

text:
Values are verbally constructed, continuous patterns of activity that are personally, intrinsically rewarding (Wilson & Sandoz, 2008). The act of engaging in valued behavior is what produces motivation for further behavior in line with that value. As such, values are directions that guide behavior, as opposed to discrete behavioral goals. They are qualities of actions, such as being kind, or brave, or acting with a sense of integrity. For example, people who valued parenting might set themselves a goal of spending 30 minutes, four times per week, engaging in a preferred activity with their child.

Individuals who struggle with anxiety and trauma may encounter many barriers to valued living. Worry and rumination may make it difficult to engage in valued action in the present moment. For example, a man who values connection in relationships may spend so much time ruminating about his behavior in a past relationship or worrying about making the same mistakes that he fails to pursue a relationship in the here and now. Or the same individual might be so fused with the ideal of having a "perfect" relationship or "getting it right" that he is not psychologically flexible enough to function well in his current relationships. Feelings of guilt or shame related to past trauma might lead to an avoidance of commitment and intimacy.

In short, valued action often entails contact with avoided thoughts, emotions, urges, and physical sensations. Values can provide a context of meaning and purpose to motivate the difficult work of finding new ways to relate to these challenging experiences.

metadata.culture_notes: Distinguishes values (directions) from goals (destinations). Important for veterans who may have lost sense of purpose after military service.
